In the current revision, chemical and catalyst waste streams are individually reported, in addition to others. Waste disposal costs were separated into two categories: non-hazardous and hazardous waste. Non-hazardous waste is disposed of at a rate of $41.88/tonne ($38.00/ton). Hazardous waste is disposed of at a rate of $88.16/tonne ($80.00/ton). 59 COST AND PERFORMANCE BASELINE FOR FOSSIL ENERGY PLANTS VOLUME 1: BITUMINOUS COAL AND NATURAL GAS TO ELECTRICITY 2.7.2.6 Co-Products and By-Products By-product quantities were also determined similarly to the consumables. However, due to the variable marketability of these by-products, specifically gypsum and sulfur, no credit was taken for their potential salable value. It should be noted that by-product credits and/or disposal costs could potentially be an additional determining factor in the choice of technology for some companies and in selecting some sites. A high local value of the product can establish whether added capital should be included in the plant costs to produce a particular co-product. Slag is a potential by-product in certain markets. Similarly, ash may also be a potential by-product in certain markets; however, due to the ACI in the PC cases, the fly ash may not be marketable. As stated above, these material streams are considered waste in this report with a concomitant disposal cost. 2.7.3 CO Transport and Storage 2 The cost of CO T&S in a deep saline formation is estimated using the Fossil Energy (FE)/NETL 2 CO Transport Cost Model (CO Transport Cost Model) and the FE/NETL CO Saline Storage Cost 2 2 2 Model (CO Storage Cost Model). Additional detail on development of these costs is available in 2 the 2019 revision of the QGESS document “Carbon Dioxide Transport and Storage Costs in NETL Studies.” [51] Due to the variances in the geologic formations that make up saline formations across the United States, the cost to store CO will vary depending on location.
